Wang Meng 葛稚川移居圖 · motion study

The Motion Budget

Seven clips, four controls, three of my own claims retracted — and then the whole instrument set aside. A diffusion model spends a fixed appetite for movement on whatever it finds most alive, and painted water never wins that contest. But moving a few ink lines is the oldest solved problem in animation, and a cel-style stroke cycle beats the model on every measure that matters, in four seconds on a laptop.

14 Aug 2026 7 renders 4 controls A100 SXM4 80GB $1.15 GPU HunyuanVideo 1.5 I2V 720p

What to take away

Naming a thing in the prompt does not make that thing move. The model allocates motion to the most animate content it can find, and in this painting that is always Ge Hong and his deer — it redraws his face into a different man while the river sits perfectly still, even when the prompt only mentions water.

The fix is not wording and not guidance strength. It is removing the competition: crop the conditioning image down to water alone, animate that, composite it back through a mask. The river then moves 9.7× harder than the rest of the frame and Ge Hong is frozen to 0.001 churn.

Superseded — read this first

The model was the wrong instrument

Ryan, on reading the above: “this is one of the most basic solved problems from even the most early animation — they would just have maybe five frames that gently switch between each other.” He is right, and it is a category error on my part. Everything below the fold still holds as a description of what a video model does to a Yuan scroll. It is no longer the recommended path.

Worse than unnecessary: a video model interpolates smoothly at 24fps, and smoothness is precisely what stops drawn water reading as drawn. Ink animation runs on twos or threes.

Retracted

The “11% drift floor” was a colour fade

Yesterday I told you every clip loses about 11% of the painting over 73 frames and called it a floor. That framing implied damage spread across the picture. It is mostly one correctable defect.

Mechanism. The sampler desaturates the whole frame as it runs — median ΔS of −0.0196 measured away from anything that moves. Silk-survival scores pixels against a colour band fixed on frame 0, so a uniform fade walks borderline pixels out of the band everywhere at once. Matching each frame's saturation back to frame 0 takes the control from 89.4% to 99.1% in three seconds of CPU.

Confirmed

The metric can be gamed, and I caught it by running the failure through it

Before believing that colour correction, I fed it yesterday's catastrophe — the clip where the painting became a photographic waterfall. It scored 102.2%. Higher than the source painting.

Mechanism. Tone-lock manipulates precisely the saturation statistics silk-survival measures, so it defeats the metric on any input, destroyed or not. The verdict is visible rather than numerical: on a clip whose content survived, the correction restores the red pine cones and green needles; on the destroyed clip it produces lurid green and magenta fringing and the waterfall is still a photograph. Tone-lock is a colour correction applied last, never a repair, and never before a measurement.

Confirmed

The model destroys Ge Hong without being asked

The control clip's prompt was “the image is completely still. no camera movement. nothing moves.” at cfg 3. It still animated the protagonist.

Mechanism. No word triggered this. The conditioning image contains a human face and an animal, the two most heavily trained subject classes in any video model, and those priors fire on sight. Over 73 frames Wang Meng's sparse downcast profile walks toward the model's own idea of an old man: heavier brows, a full moustache, the gaze lifting to camera. The deer's antlers become crosshatch and its legs stipple away. This is the same failure as the photographic waterfall — the model's prior overriding the painting — but triggered by image content instead of by a word.

Control clip, where the change landedshare of all changeper-pixel

The figures change 3.5× harder per pixel than anything else. But the landscape is not frozen either — slight change over 91.5% of the frame outweighs severe change over 8.5%, which is why stencilling the figures back recovered only 1.6 points of survival and sent me looking for the fade above.

Confirmed

Segmentation cannot cut water in this painting

SAM cut the figures and the foliage beautifully in 22 seconds. Pointed at the river it returned the two rocks sitting in the river. Pointed at the cascade it returned the bridge trestle.

Mechanism. Segmentation finds objects by their contours. Wang Meng painted water as 留白 — unpainted silk, an absence between drawn things — and an absence has no contour, so the only thing with an edge nearby gets cut instead. The fix is to define the mask by the material: bright, low-variance ground is silk; dark, locally busy is ink. That threshold follows the painting's own logic and cuts the river correctly.

Retracted

“cfg is the volume knob” — wrong, and a control caught it

Mid-session I told you there is no guidance setting at which the words both preserve the painting and direct the motion. It was a tidy mechanism and two later clips refuted it.

What refuted it. Clip C named leaves at cfg 3 on the full frame and steered strongly — selectivity 6.76. So the text channel is not off at cfg 3. Then clip F ran the water prompt at cfg 3 on a crop and moved the water as much as cfg 6 did. So guidance was never the lever at all.

Confirmed

The crop is the lever, because motion is a contest

On the full frame the prompt said “the water flows and ripples” and the water moved less than average while the figures burned. Remove the figures from the frame and the same words work.

Mechanism. The model has a limited appetite for motion and spends it on whatever it reads as most animate. Faces and animals win by default. Foliage can compete — naming leaves both moved them and halved the figure hijack, as though the budget were reallocated. Painted water cannot compete at all: it is a few dry lines on bare silk, the weakest possible cue. Cropping the people out is not a trick for safety, it removes the rival.

The motion is drift, not flicker

The ripple lines travel as a group while the rock stays put. That distinction matters because a whole-image pan would look similar in a strip — but a pan would light up the rock edges in the heatmap above, and they are black.

Corrected

The ink does not get heavier — it gets reorganised

Looking at clip E I told myself the brushwork had thickened and gone bolder than Wang Meng's dry stroke. Measured, that is false: ink darkness is identical at 107 → 107 and coverage is flat.

What actually changes. The same quantity of ink is redistributed. Counting connected strokes in the water region tells three different stories, and only one of them preserves the painter's economy.

Stroke organisation, water regionstrokes f0strokes f72mean length f0mean length f72

D — cfg 6, motion wording8526224134

D merges strokes into fewer, longer lines. E multiplies them — it adds ripple arcs Wang Meng never painted, which is what I misread as “bolder”. F alone keeps the count and length the painter chose.

Confirmed

Never put the medium's own qualities in the negative prompt

To stop E's extra arcs I added “bold ink, heavy brushwork, dark outlines” to the negative. Clip G lost 54.3% of its ink and the motion sprayed across the rocks as well — aim ratio collapsed to 1.32.

Mechanism. Dark outlines are Wang Meng's line. Suppressing them suppressed the painting. The negative prompt may name the wrong medium — photograph, film grain, 3d render — but never the qualities of the right one.

Confirmed

Composited back, the painting holds and only the water lives

The animated crop scales back into its rectangle and shows through the material-cut mask over an otherwise motionless plate. The seam is invisible at the box edge and Ge Hong is completely still.

Confirmed

Twenty minutes of arithmetic beats the rented A100

Lift the ripple lines off the silk, inpaint the ground behind them, displace them with a wave that is periodic in time, hold each drawing for two frames. Four seconds on CPU, and it loops.

The difference that generates all the others: the model redraws the strokes, the cycle moves Wang Meng's own ink. Stroke count is conserved because no stroke is ever synthesised.

Three bugs, none of them visible in a metric

It smeared the rocks. Treating every dark pixel in the water mask as a stroke displaced the rocks too and inpainted them away. The fix is the definition of a brushstroke: a line is thin. Filter on distance-to-edge and the rocks — 20 of them — stay where the painter put them.

The lines came out fainter than the source. A thresholded matte under-estimated ink coverage, so every stroke was composited with silk mixed back into it. Since the background behind the ink is known once it is inpainted, the matte is determined rather than guessed. Round-trip error at zero displacement is now 0.09 levels, and the script asserts it on every run.

The loop popped. My drift ramped across the cycle and snapped back. Fixing it forced the better model: a travelling wave, where each point moves in a small ellipse as the crest passes. That is what water does, what an animator draws, and it closes the cycle by construction.

What the cycle structurally cannot do

It cannot invent a stroke. A real animator draws ripples that form, travel and dissipate; this conserves ink exactly, so no new ripple ever appears. Over three seconds that reads as shimmer and is fine. Over a long hold it may read as a loop. Clip E — which added arcs Wang Meng never painted, written up above as a fidelity failure — is the one behaviour the deterministic method lacks.

Where Resolve fits

Fusion carries all of this natively: Paint for drawing new lines by hand, Displace with Fast Noise for warp fields, Perturb to jitter any parameter (the hand-drawn boil), Grid and Mesh Warp for shaped deformation. The split that makes sense is to design the look interactively on one shot in Fusion, then encode those numbers into the script for the other fifty. Art direction wants a GUI; production wants repeatability.

What this does to the architecture

Water, foliage and mist all look deterministic now. The camera was already render-parallax.py. On current evidence the diffusion model's remaining job on this film is character motion — the one thing it actively destroys.

Confirmed

Foliage is a different physics, and needs a different mode

The other half of the brief. Water carries a crest through a flat surface; a branch does not. A branch is a cantilever — it pivots at the trunk, amplitude grows toward the tip, and a gust reaches the base before the leaves. Applying the water field to a tree slides the canopy sideways like a sticker, which is the tell that betrays cheap 2.5D foliage.

And a different mode. Water gets lift: extract the strokes, inpaint the silk, move them over it — correct because the ground is blank and because the rocks in the river must not move. Foliage gets warp: displace the region bodily. The first attempt lifted the leaves and washed the cliff behind them out, because the ground there is textured rock that cannot be reconstructed and does not need to be.

Two dead ends worth recording. The obvious way to separate leaf from cliff is colour, and it fails twice on measurement here: cliff ink is more saturated than the foliage (0.294 vs 0.239), and only 0.9% of the leaf ink falls in the green–cyan hue band. Wang Meng's teal reads as teal in context, not in absolute pixels. Warping makes the question unnecessary.

The toolbox as it now stands

mask-bare-ground
box → a mask of the unpainted ground, cut by material rather than contour. Exists because segmentation cannot see an absence.
animate-strokes
still + mask → a looping clip. --field wave|sway, --mode lift|warp. Self-tests fidelity on every run.
composite-shot
plate + N animated regions → one shot, everything else frozen.
render-parallax
already in the repo: the camera move, applied afterwards where the transform is known.

Seconds per clip, on a laptop, and every clip loops. The diffusion path is retained in this document as a record of what a video model does to a Yuan scroll, not as a route anyone should take.

The recipe as it stands

Living water — the diffusion route, if ever needed again

frame
Crop the conditioning image so no face or animal is in it. This is the load-bearing step.
cfg
3. Six buys no extra motion once cropped, and costs line fidelity.
positive
Motion only, no style words. “the river water flows and ripples slowly downstream. the camera does not move.”
negative
Wrong-medium terms only — photograph, video footage, 3d render. Never ink, brushwork or outlines.
frames
73 at 24fps. Longer is untested.
after
tone-lock the clip, then composite. Reversing that order re-animates the frozen plate and destroys selectivity.
camera
Locked. Any move belongs to render-parallax.py afterwards, where the transform is known rather than guessed — which is also what keeps a static mask registered for all 73 frames.

What is still open

Foliage confines badly. The tree responds at full frame, but its leaves travel across a tight mask boundary, so it wants the same crop treatment as water — untested.

Branch topology is re-invented rather than displaced. Whether that reads as wind or as morphing at full speed is a judgement your eyes have to make on living-tree.mp4.

Duration beyond three seconds, and whether clips can be chained or looped, remain untested.

The cascade under the bridge is too small and too tangled with trestle to cut cleanly. The upper river carried this whole study.

Nothing here animates Ge Hong deliberately. Every result so far is about stopping him from moving.

Seven renders on one A100 SXM4 80GB, destroyed at the end of the session. $1.15 total. Crops render in 3.5 min against 10 min for a full vertical frame, which is why the crop arm could afford four variants and a control.

Scripts, masks and clips in jobs/wang-meng/motion/. Every number above came from a measurement on a rendered file; the three retractions came from building the control first.
